Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN), a global e-commerce, cloud infrastructure, and digital advertising platform, closed at $245.63, up 2.20%. Phillip Securities upgraded the stock to "buy" and raised its price target, while investors are watching demand for AWS (Amazon Web Services) and AI spending.
Trading volume reached 57.7 million shares, coming in about 51% above its three-month average of 38.3 million shares. Amazon IPO'd in 1997 and has grown 250,755% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) closed at 7,542, down 0.50%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) finished at 25,164, down 1.07%. Among internet retail, digital advertising, and logistics services peers, Walmart closed at $127.69, up 3.38%, and Costco Wholesale closed at $1,040.55, up 2.79%, underscoring a mixed retail backdrop.

What this means for investors

On Monday, Amazon regained positive momentum after the stock slid following the online retail and cloud services giant's earnings report last week. Phillip Securities is one Wall Street firm that said to buy that dip. Analyst Helena Wang raised her rating after boosting fiscal 2027 revenue estimates. She also raised her firm's price target by $10 to $330 per share.

The firm focused on the strength of Amazon's cloud demand, which was highlighted in the company's earnings report last week. AWS segment sales jumped 39% year over year to $46 billion, marking the fastest pace of growth in nearly five years. Operating income also surged 61%, amid a growing backlog.

AI-related capital spending and cash outflows led to an initial negative reaction, but investors were buying that dip today.

title: Amazon vs. Alibaba: Two E-Commerce Giants, a Big Valuation Gap, but Which Offers More Upside in 2027?
detail:
Amazon vs. Alibaba: Two E-Commerce Giants, a Big Valuation Gap, but Which Offers More Upside in 2027?
RJ Fulton, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 2:50 PM MST 5 min read
AMZN
BABA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Can Western dominance in cloud and commerce outperform Eastern scale and a cheaper valuation? Choosing between Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Alibaba (NYSE:BABA) requires weighing domestic growth against international expansion.

Amazon focuses on logistics and cloud infrastructure to serve global consumers and enterprises. Alibaba leverages its vast ecosystem in China and emerging markets to facilitate trade and cloud services. Investors often compare them as the primary titans of their respective regions, each offering unique paths to long-term growth.

The case for Amazon.com

Amazon operates a massive logistics network and online marketplace, serving millions of global consumers through its dominance among retail stocks and cloud services. Its revenue comes from online retail, third-party seller services, advertising, cloud infrastructure, and Prime subscriptions, providing several sources of growth across consumer and enterprise markets.

In FY 2025, Amazon generated $716.9 billion in revenue, an increase of 12.4% year over year. Net income reached $77.7 billion, resulting in a profit margin of approximately 10.8%. Growth was supported by its retail operations and Amazon Web Services (AWS), which reported a 20% increase in annual sales as demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure continued to expand.

Amazon ended 2025 with a current ratio of approximately 1.1x and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.4x when including lease liabilities. Free cash flow totaled $11.2 billion, down from $38.2 billion in 2024, as the company substantially increased capital spending on AI infrastructure. While these investments are weighing on near-term cash generation, they could strengthen Amazon's long-term position in cloud computing and artificial intelligence.

The case for Alibaba

Alibaba operates one of China's largest e-commerce and cloud computing platforms, serving consumers and businesses through Taobao, Tmall, and Alibaba Cloud. The company also maintains a growing international presence through platforms such as AliExpress, Lazada, and Alibaba.com, providing exposure to online retail, digital services, and enterprise technology markets.

In FY 2026, Alibaba generated $148.4 billion in revenue, an increase of 2.7% year over year. However, excluding businesses sold during the year, revenue increased approximately 11%, reflecting stronger growth across its continuing operations. Net income reached $14.8 billion, down approximately 19% from the prior year, resulting in a profit margin of 10%. The results highlight Alibaba's continued business expansion alongside pressure on profitability.

title: Amazon (AMZN) Stock for the Next 10 Years: Buy, Hold, or Avoid?
detail:
Amazon (AMZN) Stock for the Next 10 Years: Buy, Hold, or Avoid?
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool

AMZN
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), the world's largest e-commerce and cloud infrastructure company, has delivered an impressive 534% gain over the past ten years. But does its stock still have more upside potential over the next decade?

What are Amazon's biggest catalysts?

Amazon generates most of its revenue from its e-commerce business, but its cloud platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS), brings in most of its operating profits.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Over the past ten years, AWS' annual revenue jumped from $7.9 billion to $128.8 billion, while its operating margin expanded from 19.2% to 35.4%. AWS' surging profits enabled Amazon to expand its Prime ecosystem with more discounts, hardware devices, streaming media services, and other loss-leading strategies. It's already locked in more than 200 million Prime subscribers worldwide, which gives it a wide moat against other online and brick-and-mortar retailers.

AWS already hosts tens of millions of websites and apps, and it's helping its developers build and train new generative AI apps on platforms like Bedrock and SageMaker. Amazon has also been producing its own first-party AI accelerators, and it owns nearly a fifth of Anthropic -- the rapidly growing AI company that plans to go public by the end of 2026.

All of those AI catalysts for AWS -- along with the expansion of its e-commerce business into higher-growth overseas markets and the growth of its higher-margin advertising business -- could drive its earnings growth over the next decade.

What are Amazon's biggest challenges?

Amazon's growth rates are impressive, but its expansion will be costly. It expects its capex to reach $220 billion in 2026 (up from $131.8 billion in 2025) and to rise further in 2027. That increased spending -- and competition from other hyperscalers -- could compress AWS' margins. That pressure could also make it tougher for Amazon to expand its lower-margin retail business.

Rising interest rates will make it more expensive for Amazon to expand its AI infrastructure, reduce the market's demand for its cloud services, and compress its valuation. Inflation, which has been exacerbated by the Iran war and the Trump Administration's unpredictable tariffs, could also throttle the growth of its retail business (including Whole Foods).

Apple posts stronger-than-expected Q4 revenue in first earnings report for new CEO John Ternus

Apple Inc. posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal fourth quarter, giving new CEO John Ternus an upbeat start to his tenure, which began in September. The solid results bucked a downward trend for tech giants this quarter, as companies including Alphabet, Amazon and Intel had disappointing quarterly results.

The Cupertino, California-based company earned $30.71 billion, or $2.10 per share, in the July-September period. That's up 12% from $27.47 billion, or $1.85 per share, in the same period a year earlier. Apple said its earnings included 5 cents per share from tariff refunds.

Revenue rose 12% to $114.5 billion from $102.5 billion.

Analysts, on average, were expecting earnings of $1.99 per share on revenue of $113.4 billion, according to a poll by FactSet.

Apple recently hiked its prices partly due to a global memory chip shortage brought on by the artificial intelligence boom, which helped drive revenue. Compared with earlier generations, the iPhone 18 costs about $100 more and the price of Macs and iPads also increased in June.

"Apple's strong earnings come in the wake of a recent tech sell-off, as investors question the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom driven by Apple's Big Tech counterparts," said Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne, adding that record iPhone revenue and strong growth in China demonstrate the resilience of Apple's business.

While its rivals are facing investor uncertainty over massive investments in artificial intelligence, Bourne said Apple's "tepid approach" to AI infrastructure spending helps preserve its cash flow — while partnerships with companies like Alphabet could help Apple to strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers.

The iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable phone that starts at $1,999, was not yet on sale during the company's fiscal fourth quarter, so it wasn't included in the earnings results. Demand has been strong for the pricey model, even though some users have reported problems that include cracked screens, which Apple is fixing or replacing. Apple is also dealing with supply constraints for the Duo, which went on sale in October, though current earliest shipping dates are for January.

Apple's shares were flat in after-hours trading. The stock had closed down 1.8% at $338.32 in regular trading.

title: Is Amazon Stock a Buy as Cloud Revenue Continues to Surge?

Is Amazon Stock a Buy as Cloud Revenue Continues to Surge?
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool

AMZN
NVDA

Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) turned in another strong quarter when it reported its third-quarter results after the bell on Oct. 29. However, the stock's struggle to gain momentum continued, as it has largely run in place this year. Despite continued strong revenue and earnings growth, Amazon stock is up only modestly in 2026 and has risen only around 45% over the past five years in a strong bull market.

While Amazon has been a market laggard in recent years, I think now could be a great time to buy the stock. Let's take a closer look at its Q3 results and prospects to see why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The path to $1 trillion in AWS revenue

Amazon's cloud computing unit, AWS, once again led the way for the company in Q3. AWS revenue soared more than 39% to $46 billion, topping the $45.3 billion consensus, as compiled by StreetAccount. It was its fastest growth in nearly five years, an acceleration from last quarter's 37% growth.

The company highlighted the strength of the Bedrock inference service, noting that Fortune 500 companies are spending nearly seven times as much on Bedrock as last year. Meanwhile, token volumes have increased nearly 17-fold. It noted that it recently added OpenAI models to Bedrock, and that usage has grown rapidly.

Amazon said its chip business more than doubled in the quarter. Revenue commitments for both Graviton (its custom ARM Holdings-based CPU) and Trainium (its AI accelerator), meanwhile, have increased more than 20-fold year over year. Given high demand, Amazon will also start selling Trainium chips outside of AWS starting in late 2027.

Operating income in the segment, meanwhile, jumped 56% to $17.8 billion. Investments in custom chips and networking helped it achieve a strong 38.7% operating margin in the quarter

Amazon's e-commerce operation, meanwhile, continues to perform well. Its North American sales rose by 6% year over year to $112.9 billion, while international sales rose 5%, or 8% in constant currencies, to $43.1 billion. The solid growth came despite a shift in Prime Day from Q3 last year into Q2 this year. It said excluding this shift, e-commerce growth would have been 4% higher.

On the negative side, the company saw a major slowdown in advertising revenue growth. Ad revenue grew 12% in the quarter to $19.6 billion. That was a big deceleration from the 26% growth it saw in Q2. However, management said the shift in Prime Day had an 8.5% sequential impact.
